description: Merhaba! Biz FLOW, Balıkesir Üniversitesi’nden mühendislik öğrencilerinden oluşan bir ekibiz. NASA Space Apps Bursa’da “Uzay Görevlerindeki Astronotlar İçin Sağlık İzleme Yazılımı” üzerinde çalışıyoruz.
summary: Hello, we are Flow! We are the creators of Orbitalis ASTRA. We developed this software specifically for the 'Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions' category of the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our software is a user-friendly health data collection platform that adapts to today's technological standards, effectively utilizing modern technologies to interpret data with AI and present actionable insights to the end user. It is designed to operate functionally for astronauts experiencing significant communication delays with Earth during deep space missions.
details:
What it does and how it works

Orbitalis is a crew health console for a six-person Mars mission (ARES-1, Mission Day 180). Three astronauts are in Mars orbit and three are on the surface in EVA suits. A message to Earth can take up to 22 minutes one way, so the crew cannot wait for the flight surgeon. ASTRA-MED OS monitors 36 metrics in 5 data groups for every astronaut, live, and works in two layers:

Layer 1 (onboard, no internet): It learns each astronaut’s personal baseline from their first 30 readings. It then flags deviations with directional z-scores and checks NASA limits (NASA-STD-3001, OCHMO), raising CAUTION and WARNING alerts. Three pre-approved safe actions run on their own: storm shelter ingress, increased ventilation and mandatory crew rest. Every action is logged, and the crew acknowledges it.

Layer 2, ASTRA (AI): ASTRA explains every alert and answers crew questions using only the live data. It shows source links and checks every number in its answer against the data. It never diagnoses, never recommends medication, and cannot raise or change alerts. Without internet it falls back to rule-based answers.

The interface has these screens:

Mission Status: the whole mission at a glance.

Astronaut View: a 3D body map with head, chest, lower body and environment regions.

Helmet visor HUD: for the EVA crew, with voice decisions.

Reports: the incident log.

Fatigue tests: NASA-TLX, Samn-Perelli and the 3-minute PVT-B.

Benefits

Problems are caught earlier. Alerts are personal: each astronaut is compared with their own normal, not one population threshold.

The crew can act during the comms delay. A safe first response starts on board without waiting for Earth.

Decisions stay with people. AI explanations make alerts easier to understand, while the crew and the flight surgeon still decide.

Every number can be checked. Each value on screen links to its source, and values without a published source are labeled “Assumption.”

Intended impact

We want to support Earth-independent medical operations for long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars. The same approach could serve analog missions and other isolated crews. The next step is to connect real wearable sensors and a live link to the flight surgeon.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

Code: TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, three.js (3D astronaut) and Recharts. Tests use Vitest (176 automated tests) and oxlint.

ASTRA: Google Gemini (gemini-3.8-flash, with backup models), running in a server function with 10 read-only tools.

Deployment: Vercel, with Cloudflare Workers and GitHub Pages as backups.

AI used in development: Anthropic Claude and Google Gemini. The team reviewed and tested all generated code.

Hardware: none. All sensor data is simulated.

License: open source under Apache 2.0.

NASA data and resources we used:

DONKI: event times of the real May 2024 solar storm.

NASA SDO footage (SVS 5286): the X3.9 flare.

OSDR Environmental Data App: ISS cabin data.

Limits and risks: NASA-STD-3001 and OCHMO technical briefs, Human Research Program risks, Curiosity RAD dose rates and Mars DRA 5.0.

Other: NASA-TLX, and the astronaut model from NASA 3D Resources.

How it is creative

The solar storm is real. The solar particle event scenario replays the May 2024 storm with NASA’s own event times and imagery.

Personal baselines replace fixed thresholds.

Safe automation and AI explanation are kept apart. Deterministic code acts; the AI only explains.

The surface crew sees alerts in their helmet visor and answers by voice.

Five scenarios let the jury see the whole system in action: nominal day, solar particle event, Mars Day 180, CO₂ scrubber failure and EVA overexertion.

Factors our team considered

Communication delay and crew autonomy.

Medical AI safety: no diagnosis, no medication advice, AI is read-only, and there is a safety filter.

Transparency: sourced numbers, labeled assumptions, and a disclosure of all AI and libraries used.

Privacy: all crew data is synthetic, and no real astronaut’s health data is used.

Alarm fatigue and accessibility: red is used only for WARNING, and every level shows color, symbol and text together.

Offline operation.

Teamwork: we split the work into four parts (simulation, Layer 1, interface, ASTRA) around a shared data contract.
